title: The Geopolitics of Critical Minerals: Navigating Scarcity, Concentration, and Control
gist: BCG argues China is the only integrated critical-minerals superpower, holding over half of global processing in 16 of 23 mapped minerals, and that Western diversification (policy measures up 367% since the pandemic, $65B public finance announced) will be slow because corporate investment fell in 2025 and the IEA sees no major processing deconcentration within ten years. Extraction countries' dependence on China rose 15 points in five years, while US equity stakes, stockpiles and allied blocs like FORGE point to bifurcated supply chains.

insights.claim: China is the only integrated superpower in critical minerals: it holds more than half of global processing share in 16 of 23 mapped critical minerals and one-third or more in 3 others, and outproduces the rest of the world domestically in 8 of 23 in extraction.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Leverage sits in midstream refining, not mines, so mine-count diversification stories overstate real supply security.
insights.quote: China possesses more than half the global share of 16 minerals, and one-third or more of 3 others
insights.locator: A Unipolar Critical Minerals Landscape

insights.claim: China's dominance was deliberate and long-horizon: rare earths appeared in its 1981 five-year plan, followed by low-cost financing, export quotas, Made in China 2025 (70% domestic inputs target), overseas mine acquisitions, and a March 2026 five-year plan prioritizing self-sufficiency over mere supply security.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Expect China to keep tightening vertical integration; Western catch-up must be measured in decades, not budget cycles.
insights.locator: China's Strength Is Not by Accident but by Design

insights.claim: China extracts gallium, germanium and vanadium as byproducts of base-metal processing and steel smelting, so its heavy industry gives it cheap, hard-to-replicate minor-metal supply.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Minor metals tied to others' byproduct streams are structurally cheap for China and uneconomic standalone for others.
insights.locator: A Unipolar Critical Minerals Landscape

insights.claim: China's export controls target 'mosquito' minerals: small by market size but critical across sectors, where China leads in both extraction and processing. It still controls 16 minerals including 7 medium and heavy rare earths despite the trade truce extension.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The truce is reversible tariff-for-controls trading, so controls on small-cap critical inputs remain a standing tail risk for defense and electronics supply chains.
insights.quote: These are usually “mosquitoes”—not large by market size, but highly critical across sectors
insights.locator: The Race to Diversify Supply Chains

insights.claim: China is mirroring the US semiconductor-export-control playbook by institutionalizing export controls on minerals, and has added company- and industry-specific bans (e.g. defense sectors) that already caused delays and temporary shortages.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Chokepoint warfare is now symmetric; supply-chain risk pricing should include politically targeted denial, not just volatility.
insights.locator: The Race to Diversify Supply Chains

insights.claim: Extraction powerhouses (the Big Nine) have not built processing capacity, and their dependence on China for exporting raw critical minerals rose by 15 percentage points over five years, so resource wealth is deepening rather than loosening Chinese lock-in.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Mining-jurisdiction exposure is not a hedge against China if the ore must go there for refining.
insights.locator: A Unipolar Critical Minerals Landscape

insights.claim: The Industrial Five manufacturers (EU, Japan, South Korea, UK, US) are large net importers of raw and processed minerals and rely on China's midstream processing, compounding their dependence.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Western industrials' margin and uptime risk sits in processing steps they do not own.
insights.locator: A Unipolar Critical Minerals Landscape

insights.claim: Apparent supplier diversification is often illusory: many supposedly alternative sources remain tied to the same state or have financing connections to it, and leading Chinese processors are investing in capacity abroad, muddying who depends on whom.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Diligence on supply chains should trace ownership and financing, not just geography of origin.
insights.quote: many supposedly alternative sourcing options remain tied to the same state or have financing connections with it
insights.locator: Actions for Business Leaders

themes.theme: Demand surge from AI, defense and energy

insights.claim: Critical-mineral demand is accelerating on four fronts: AI data centers (IEA expects capacity to double by 2030, lifting gallium, germanium and silicon metal demand), defense (an F-35 needs more than ten critical minerals), energy (EV battery demand up more than 150% by 2030), and infrastructure.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: AI capex adds a minerals-supply constraint on top of power and chips, favoring non-China processing assets.
insights.locator: Geopolitics Is Affecting Demand for Critical Minerals

insights.claim: BCG expects demand growth to outpace critical mineral supply over the coming decade, making dependable access a matter of national power.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Structural deficit plus political pricing implies persistent premium for secure-supply assets.
insights.quote: This powerful acceleration of demand is likely to outpace critical mineral supplies in the coming decade.
insights.locator: Geopolitics Is Affecting Demand for Critical Minerals

insights.claim: The IEA estimates the world will need more than $500 billion for mining and $200 billion for processing of energy-related critical minerals by 2040.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Sizes the capital pool needed; processing is the smaller but scarcer-skilled leg.
insights.locator: The Race to Diversify Supply Chains

insights.claim: Policy measures affecting critical minerals rose 367% since the pandemic and hit a record in 2025, with tools once seen as unconventional now standard.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Government is becoming a principal in this market; policy flow is a leading indicator for asset values.
insights.locator: The Race to Diversify Supply Chains

insights.claim: The US is taking supply-side equity and demand-side guarantees: the Pentagon put $400 million into MP Materials for rare earth processing and magnets at Mountain Pass, defense procurement mandates create demand, and Project Vault is a public-private stockpile that aggregates demand to stabilize the market.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Offtake mandates and stockpiling put a floor under non-China producers, shifting risk from commodity price to policy.
insights.locator: The Race to Diversify Supply Chains

insights.claim: Allied coordination is institutionalizing: the US-convened FORGE seeks a plurilateral preferential trade zone shielding producers from outside competition and price swings, while the G7 alliance targets under 60% dependence on any single non-allied country for rare earths and permanent magnets by 2030 and 50% as soon as possible. The EU is discussing a European Corporation on Critical Raw Materials, and Japan is debating expanding JOGMEC's role.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A price-protected allied bloc implies bifurcated pricing between China-linked and allied supply.
insights.locator: The Race to Diversify Supply Chains

insights.claim: Trade geopolitics now directly trades minerals: the September 2026 Xi visit extended a truce where China suspended some export controls for lower US tariffs, China limited exports to Japan in early 2026, the US asked Canada for right of first refusal, and minerals feature in Ukraine reconstruction talks.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Minerals are a bargaining chip in bilateral deals, so event risk clusters around diplomatic flashpoints.
insights.locator: Geopolitics Is Affecting Demand for Critical Minerals

insights.claim: Announced public finance for critical minerals reached $65 billion, up fourfold since 2023, yet corporate investment in critical minerals production fell in 2025 per the IEA; announcements do not guarantee disbursement.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The gap between announced public money and actual private capex suggests supply response lags headlines; fade announcement-driven rallies.
insights.quote: Paradoxically, investment by companies in critical minerals production actually decreased in 2025
insights.locator: The Race to Diversify Supply Chains

insights.claim: China is protecting its position by export-controlling processing technology and know-how, so the IEA does not expect processing concentration in key minerals to change significantly over the next ten years.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Assume China-centered processing through 2036; non-China capacity will be capital- and talent-constrained.
insights.locator: The Race to Diversify Supply Chains

insights.claim: BCG concludes the landscape is unlikely to shift fundamentally soon, so concentration, scarcity and heavy government involvement are the baseline.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Treat minerals policy risk as permanent, not cyclical, in strategic planning.
insights.quote: The critical minerals landscape is unlikely to shift fundamentally anytime soon.
insights.locator: Strategic Imperatives for Business Leaders and Policymakers

themes.theme: Global South leverage and resource nationalism

insights.claim: Supplier countries use three tools: value capture (Indonesia's 2020 raw nickel export ban, followed by the DRC and others; renegotiated Sicomines deal), revenue raising (royalties, export duties, Indonesia's single export window), and price influencing (export quotas, strategic reserves), though price tools are limited by reliance on external capital, technology and processing.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Expect rising resource-nationalism risk premia in mining jurisdictions, with policy discretion over terms.
insights.locator: Intensifying Competition in the Global South

insights.claim: Processing requires knowledge, technology, talent, capital, water and power, so processing hubs may emerge in places with less dominant extraction, such as Malaysia, Morocco and the Gulf states, leveraging ties to the Industrial Five.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Midstream refining investments in swing jurisdictions may beat mining-country plays on value capture.
insights.locator: Intensifying Competition in the Global South

insights.claim: The West is competing with China in Africa through bilateral preferential-access and security deals, including a DFC financing package of more than $500 million plus EU support for the Lobito rail corridor carrying DRC minerals to western ports.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Logistics corridors are the investable chokepoint of Africa's western-aligned supply route.
insights.locator: Intensifying Competition in the Global South

insights.claim: Forcing processing too early can destroy value: an African government avoided strict processing requirements that would shrink upstream mining and instead sequenced a roadmap to grow mining first, then domestic processing.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Export-ban policies that skip sequencing risk output declines and investor flight.
insights.locator: Example Policymaker Action

insights.claim: Companies should map ownership and control across suppliers and processing nodes, then reduce exposure through substitution, product-mix changes, recycling and dual-material flexibility, treating redesign as a cost and reliability upside.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Firms with design flexibility will carry lower minerals-shock risk; ask about substitution roadmaps.
insights.locator: Actions for Business Leaders

insights.claim: One leading OEM designed its EV platform geometry, space and anchor points so REE-free motors can be swapped in once technically mature, hedging rare earth exposure without waiting for the technology.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Option-value engineering is a cheap hedge; watch for REE-free motor adoption as a demand-side threat to rare earth magnet volumes.
insights.locator: Example Business Leader Action

insights.claim: Co-investment, equity stakes and partnering with governments let companies secure long-term access without carrying the full cost or risk, and recycling also depends on partnerships and incentives to scale.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Offtake-plus-equity structures between industrials and miners are likely to proliferate.
insights.locator: Actions for Business Leaders
